description:
宇宙の専門知識はゼロ。好奇心は無限大。🚀

北海道大学の学生4人のチームです。専門はAI・自然言語処理、工学、環境科学、アントレプレナーシップ。宇宙の専門家はいません。だからこそ「宇宙を知らない人の目線」で、専門用語より先に「自分ならどう判断するか」を体験できるゲームを作りました。

「Jezero Traverse」は、NASAの探査車パーサヴィアランスのミッションを、打ち上げから岩石の採取までたどるゲームです。

・本物のデータ：NASAの実映像、JPLの軌道データ、探査車の画像と走行記録を使用
・限られた資源：迷う時間や誤った選択で電力が減り、尽きると失敗
・難しい判断：データを読んで走行を計画し、実際の故障には対応策を自由記述で回答
・最大の難所：NASAの危険度マップの上で崖や岩を避けて着陸
・選択の評価：最後に点数を出し、間違えた判断を理由とともに振り返る

宇宙ミッションを「遠い世界の話」から「自分で判断してみる体験」へ。学び、創り、星の向こうまで挑戦します！🌌
summary: Jezero Traverse is a browser game that lets players relive NASA's Perseverance mission, from launch to its early drives on Mars, using real NASA data. The prologue replays the launch, the 203-day cruise computed from JPL Horizons trajectories, and the landing with real NASA footage. Players then steer the descent across NASA's actual landing hazard map of Jezero Crater. After landing, the rover follows its real traverse from Sol 15 to Sol 23 on HiRISE maps and Navcam images. Before each drive, players read real data such as terrain tilt, local solar time, and image downlink time, and choose a drive plan while managing battery power. Along the way, they face real accidents from past rovers, such as Spirit's broken wheel, and explain how engineers solved them. The game shows that mission design is a chain of decisions under limited time, power, and information. It turns NASA's open data into something anyone can explore in a few minutes.
details:
What it does

Jezero Traverse follows Perseverance through five scenes: launch, cruise, landing, exploration, and sampling. Players can start from the launch or jump straight to the rover. The interface supports English and Japanese.

How it works

  • Launch and cruise: Real NASA launch footage, including rocket onboard cameras, plays first. The 203-day cruise is replayed in about 20 seconds. Distance, speed, and radio delay come from daily JPL Horizons data for the spacecraft, Earth, and Mars. Our computed path (470.2 million km) matches NASA's published value (472 million km) within 0.4%.
  • Landing game: From backshell separation (about 2.6 km altitude) to the sky crane, players steer over NASA's real landing hazard map (PIA23970). Red and yellow zones damage the lander, and the goal is the real landing site. Real descent video plays in a small window at the same time.
  • Rover drives: The rover replays its real traverse from Sol 15 to Sol 23. It uses seven Navcam images from NASA PDS, rover positions from PDS PLACES, the MMGIS traverse line, and HiRISE tiles from Mars Trek. The audio is the real Sol 16 driving sound recorded on Mars.
  • Drive planning: Before the Sol 16, 20, and 23 drives, players read real data from PLACES and the PDS image labels. The data includes terrain tilt, local mean solar time, sun elevation, and image downlink time. Then players choose a plan. Correct answers are calculated from the data and our game rules.
  • Power: Battery drops while thinking, after mistakes, and per meter driven and climbed. It recharges between sols, like the MMRTG. At 0%, the mission fails.
  • Real accidents: Each run includes one of five real rover accidents, such as Spirit's frozen wheel or Opportunity stuck in a dune. Players type how they would respond, and a keyword grader checks the answer.
  • Big event: A real dust devil filmed by Navcam on Sol 899 appears with a short quiz.
  • Sampling: At the goal, players aim the drill and core a rock at Bunsen Peak, shown with NASA's real coring images from Sol 1088.
  • Results: A score and rank (S to D), plus a review of each mistake with the real response.

Benefits

  • Every photo, video, recording, and mission number comes from real NASA missions. Decision thresholds, power, and scoring are game rules, and AI-generated graphics are labeled on screen.
  • Players experience why rovers stop, wait for images, and drive slowly.
  • It runs in any browser from a simple local web server, with no build step, no API key, and no internet connection needed, so it works in classrooms.

What we hope to achieve

We want students and the public to feel the real decisions behind a Mars mission. We also want to show how much open NASA data can do. Next steps: more sols and accidents, and AI-based grading of free-text answers using a local embedding model.

Tools

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (ES modules, no framework), Web Audio API for sound effects, Python for data preparation (PDS label parsing, Horizons and PLACES processing), and ffmpeg for video clips. The data-preparation scripts are kept in an earlier commit of the repository. AI tools: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Claude, and ChatGPT (see the AI section). Source code: https://github.com/yanaginagio/nasa_hackason
